knowledge_point.title: Calculating the Determinant of a 2x2 Matrix With Integer Entries

question.:question/problem:
Calculate $\text{det}(M)$, if
$M=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -9 \\ 10 & 2\end{bmatrix}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a $2\times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

$$
\begin{vmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{vmatrix}=ad-bc.
$$

Using the formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(M) & =\begin{vmatrix}-4 & -9 \\ 10 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-4\cdot 2-(-9)\cdot 10 \\  & =-8-(-90) \\  & =82\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
If
$D=\begin{bmatrix}3x & -2 \\ 6x & x+6\end{bmatrix}$
and $det(D)=-75$, what is the value of $x?$

$x=$
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a $2\times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

$$
\begin{vmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{vmatrix}=ad-bc.
$$

Using the formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(D) & =\begin{vmatrix}3x & -2 \\ 6x & x+6\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3x\cdot (x+6)-(-2)\cdot 6x \\  & =3{x}^{2}+30x\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(D)=-75$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(D) & =-75 \\ 3{x}^{2}+30x & =-75 \\ 3{x}^{2}+30x+75 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+10x+25 & =0 \\ (x+5)^{2} & =0 \\ x & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Antiderivative of a Monomial

question.:question/problem:
Calculate 

$$
\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

 Use $C$ for the arbitrary constant of integration.

{{antiderivative}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Apply the power rule with $n=2$ and include an arbitrary constant $C$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x&=\frac{x^{2+1}}{2+1}+C \\ &=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\frac{x^{3}}{3}+C\right)&=\frac{1}{3}\cdot 3x^{2}+0 \\ &=x^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$
\int \sqrt[3]{{x}^{7}}\,\text{d}x=
$$



Work on $x>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We start by writing the root as a rational power, $\sqrt[3]{{x}^{7}}={x}^{7/3}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{7}{3}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt[3]{{x}^{7}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{7/3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{7/3+1}}{(\frac{7}{3}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{10/3}}{\left(\frac{10}{3}\right)}+C \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{10/3}}{10}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{3{x}^{10/3}}{10}+C) &= \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{3{x}^{10/3}}{10}\right)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\ &= \frac{3}{10}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{10/3})+0 \\ &= \frac{3}{10}\cdot \frac{10}{3}{x}^{10/3-1} \\ &= {x}^{7/3}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{3/2}}$ and that ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x)$, calculate $F(x).$ Assume $x>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{'}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\frac{1}{{x}^{3/2}}={x}^{-3/2}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{3}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-3/2+1}}{(-\frac{3}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/2}}{\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}+C \\  & =-2{x}^{-1/2}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{{x}^{1/2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Product Containing a Trigonometric Function

question.:question/problem: Differentiate $- 3 x^{2}\tan x$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)=- 3 x^{2}$ and $v(x)=\tan{\left(x \right)}.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}(u(x)v(x))' &=u'(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot v'(x) \\ &=(- 3 x^{2})'\cdot (\tan{\left(x \right)}) \\ &\quad +(- 3 x^{2})\cdot (\tan{\left(x \right)})' \\ &=(- 6 x)(\tan{\left(x \right)}) \\ &\quad +(- 3 x^{2})(\sec^{2}{\left(x \right)}) \\ &=- 6 x \tan{\left(x \right)} \\ &\quad +(- 3 x^{2} \sec^{2}{\left(x \right)})\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Product  at a Given Point

question.:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=(2 x^{3})\cdot (\sin{\left(x \right)})$, calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=2 x^{3}$ and $v(x)=\sin{\left(x \right)}.$ Then, we have

$$
u'(x)=6 x^{2},\quad v'(x)=\cos{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx} &=uv'(x)+vu'(x) \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(2 x^{3})\cdot (\cos{\left(x \right)}) \\ &{}+(\sin{\left(x \right)})\cdot (6 x^{2})\end{aligned} \\ &=2 x^{2} \left(x \cos{\left(x \right)} + 3 \sin{\left(x \right)}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_{x=\frac{\pi}{2}} &=\begin{aligned}&(2 \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{3})\cdot (\cos{\left(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \right)}) \\ &{}+(\sin{\left(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \right)})\cdot (6 \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{2})\end{aligned} \\ &=\left(\frac{\pi^{3}}{4}\right)\cdot (0)+(1)\cdot \left(\frac{3 \pi^{2}}{2}\right) \\ &=\frac{3 \pi^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $\frac{3 \pi^{2}}{2}.$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The function is zero at $x=\pi.$
- **II.** The complete set of inputs at which the function has maximum values is $x=2n\pi.$
- **III.** The range of the function is $[-1,1].$

knowledge_point.title: Utilizing the Periodicity Property of the Cosine Function

question.:question/problem: If $\cos x=-\frac{10}{11},$ then $\cos (x-16\pi )=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The period of $y=\cos x$ is $2\pi .$ Therefore, for an integer $n$ we have

$$
\cos x=\cos (x+2n\pi ).
$$

Substituting $n=-8$ into the right-hand-side of the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\cos x &=\cos (x+2\cdot (-8)\cdot \pi )=\cos (x-16\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if $\cos x=-\frac{10}{11},$ then $\cos (x-16\pi )=-\frac{10}{11}.$

question.:question/problem:
Calculate 

$$
\displaystyle\int -4\left(\sqrt{t}\right)^{3}+4t^{2}-1\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

. Assume $t>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Rewrite as powers, apply the sum and constant factor rules, and integrate each term using $\int t^p\,\mathrm{d}t=t^{p+1}/(p+1)+C$ for $p\ne-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \int -4\left(\sqrt{t}\right)^{3}+4t^{2}-1\,\mathrm{d}t\\ &= \int\left(-4t^{\frac{3}{2}}+4t^{2}-1\right)\,\mathrm{d}t\\ &= -4\int t^{\frac{3}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}t+4\int t^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t-\int t^{0}\,\mathrm{d}t\\ &= -4\left(\frac{t^{\frac{5}{2}}}{\frac{5}{2}}\right)+4\left(\frac{t^{3}}{3}\right)-\left(\frac{t^{1}}{1}\right)+C\\ &= -\frac{8\sqrt{t^{5}}}{5}+\frac{4t^{3}}{3}-t+C\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Constructing and Solving a Dilution Model: Inflow Equals Outflow

question.:question/problem:
A nutrient-mixing tank initially holds $375\,\text{L}$ of solution containing $4\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved supplement.
A feed solution containing $0.01\,\text{kg/L}$ of the supplement is pumped into the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of $15\,\text{L/min}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of supplement in the tank $9$ minutes after pumping begins.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of supplement in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which supplement enters the tank minus the rate at which additives leave the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which supplement enters the tank.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.01\,\text{kg/L}$ of the supplement enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *supplement* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.01\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.01\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.15\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which supplement exits the tank.

Next, note that the rate of flow in equals the rate of flow out, so the volume in the tank remains $375\,\text{L}.$ Then, since $Q$ is the amount of supplement in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{375}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $15\,\text{L/min},$ *supplement* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(15\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{375}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{375}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{15Q}{375}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{25}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.15-\frac{Q}{25}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{25}Q=\frac{3}{20}.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${Q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{Q}_{c}}{dt}+\frac{1}{25}{Q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{Q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t/25},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{Q}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${Q}_{p}=\alpha$ and $\frac{d{Q}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+\frac{1}{25}\alpha =\frac{3}{20}\,⟹\,\alpha =3.75.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${Q}_{p}(t)=3.75.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
Q(t)={Q}_{c}(t)+{Q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t/25}+3.75.
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $4\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved supplement. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=4,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =4 \\ A{e}^{-0/25}+3.75 & =4 \\ A & =0.25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=3.75+0.25{e}^{-t/25}
$$

Finally,  the amount of supplement in the tank $9$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$
Q(9)=3.75+0.25{e}^{-9/25}≈3.92\,\text{kg},
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

knowledge_point.title: Constructing and Solving a Dilution Model

question.:question/problem:
A juice-processing tank initially holds $600\,\text{L}$ of liquid containing $11\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved sugar.
A solution containing $0.05\,\text{kg/L}$ of dissolved sugar is pumped into the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of $18\,\text{L/min}.$ If the amount of sugar $Q(t),$ in kilograms, in the tank $t$ minutes after pumping begins is given by

$$
Q(t)=\alpha \,(1-\frac{t}{100})+\beta {(1-\frac{t}{100})}^{3}
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants, what is the value of $\alpha -\beta ?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of dissolved substance in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. The amount entering minus the amount leaving gives
$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=Q'_{\text{in}}-Q'_{\text{out}}.
$$
The units of these rates are $\text{kg/min}.$

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which substance enters the tank.
$$
\begin{aligned}Q'_{\text{in}}&=(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot(12\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\\
&=(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\\&=0.6\,\text{kg/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which substance exits the tank.
The volume is
$$
V(t)=600+12t-18t=(600-6t)\,\text{L}.
$$
The concentration is $\frac{Q}{600-6t}\,\text{kg/L}.$ Hence,
$$
\begin{aligned}Q'_{\text{out}}&=(18\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot(\frac{Q}{600-6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\\
&=(18\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot(\frac{Q}{600-6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\\
&=\frac{18Q}{600-6t}\,\text{kg/min}=\frac{3Q}{100-t}\,\text{kg/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.
$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}&=Q'_{\text{in}}-Q'_{\text{out}}\\&=0.6-\frac{3Q}{100-t}.\end{aligned}
$$
Thus,
$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{100-t}Q=0.6.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.
This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}I(t)&=e^{\int 3/(100-t)\,dt}\\&=e^{-3\ln|100-t|}\\&=e^{\ln (100-t)^{-3}}\\&=(100-t)^{-3}.\end{aligned}
$$
Multiplying both sides by $I(t)=(100-t)^{-3}$ yields
$$
\begin{aligned}(100-t)^{-3}\cdot(\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{100-t}Q)&=(100-t)^{-3}\cdot 0.6\\
(100-t)^{-3}\frac{dQ}{dt}+3(100-t)^{-4}Q&=0.6(100-t)^{-3}\\\frac{d}{dt}(Q(100-t)^{-3})&=0.6(100-t)^{-3}.\end{aligned}
$$
Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$
$$
\begin{aligned}\int\frac{d}{dt}(Q(100-t)^{-3})\,dt&=\int 0.6(100-t)^{-3}\,dt\\Q(100-t)^{-3}&=0.6\cdot\frac{1}{2}(100-t)^{-2}+C\\Q(t)&=0.3(100-t)+C(100-t)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.
The initial condition is $Q(0)=11.$ Thus,
$$
\begin{aligned}0.3(100-0)+C(100-0)^{3}&=11\\
30+C(100)^{3}&=11\\C(100)^{3}&=-19\\C&=- \frac{19}{1000000}.\end{aligned}
$$
Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$
$$
Q(t)=- \frac{3 t}{10} - \frac{19 \left(100 - t\right)^{3}}{1000000} + 30.
$$
Writing this in the supplied normalized form gives
$$
Q(t)=30(1-\frac{t}{100})-19(1-\frac{t}{100})^{3}.
$$
Finally, we have $\alpha=30,\beta=-19,$ and
$$
\alpha-\beta=30-(-19)=49.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing an Exponential Expression

question.:question/problem:
Calculate 

$$
\int xe^{- 5 x}\,\text{d}x.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int xe^{- 5 x}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′} & =e^{- 5 x}\, & ⟹\,v=- \frac{e^{- 5 x}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot e^{- 5 x}\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \left(- \frac{e^{- 5 x}}{5}\right)-\int \left(- \frac{e^{- 5 x}}{5}\right)\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =- \frac{1}{5}\cdot xe^{- 5 x}+\frac{1}{5}\cdot \int e^{- 5 x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int xe^{- 5 x}\,\text{d}x & =- \frac{1}{5}\cdot xe^{- 5 x}+\frac{1}{5}\cdot \int e^{- 5 x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =- \frac{1}{5}\cdot xe^{- 5 x}-\frac{1}{25}\cdot e^{- 5 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Collecting the linear terms gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int xe^{- 5 x}\,\mathrm{d}x & =-\frac{x e^{- 5 x}}{5} - \frac{e^{- 5 x}}{25}+C\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Applying the Quotient Rule

question.:question/problem:
For the function

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{2 x^{2} - y^{2} - 1}{\sqrt{y}},
$$

evaluate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ at the point $(-1,4)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Hold $x$ constant and differentiate with respect to $y$. Write $N=2 x^{2} - y^{2} - 1$ and $D=\sqrt{y}$. The component derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_{y}&=- 2 y, \\
D_{y}&=\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{y}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For the square root use $D_{y}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}$.  Apply the quotient rule, keeping its subtraction and squared denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=\frac{N_{y}D-ND_{y}}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{\left(- 2 y\right)D-N\left(\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{y}}\right)}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{- 2 x^{2} - 3 y^{2} + 1}{2\left(y\right)\sqrt{y}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last step multiplies the numerator and denominator by $2\sqrt{y}$ and collects the numerator terms. Now substitute the point, after differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right|_{(-1,4)}&=\frac{\left(-8\right)\left(2\right)-\left(-15\right)\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}{\left(2\right)^2} \\
&=- \frac{49}{16}.
\end{aligned}
$$

 These expressions apply where $y>0$.

knowledge_point.title: Finding Partial Derivatives of Two-Variable Functions

question.:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as constant. First write $e^{3 x + 3 y}=e^{3 x}\cdot e^{3 y}$ to expose the held exponential factor. Apply the sum and constant multiple rules term by term.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(e^{3 x + 3 y}) &=e^{3 x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(e^{3 y}) \\
&=e^{3 x}\cdot \left(3 e^{3 y}\right) \\
&=3 e^{3 x + 3 y}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(x^{3} y^{4}) &=x^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y^{4}) \\
&=x^{3}\cdot \left(4 y^{3}\right) \\
&=4 x^{3} y^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $f_{y}(x,y)=4 x^{3} y^{3} + 3 e^{3 x + 3 y}$.

knowledge_point.title: Differentiating an Exponential Function with a Linear Exponent

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y={e}^{-1-4x}$ as the composite function

$$
y={e}^{u},\,u=-1-4x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot (-4) \\  & =-4{e}^{u} \\  & =-4{e}^{-1-4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the sum rule of differentiation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{4}-{e}^{-1-4x}) \\  & =4{x}^{3}-(-4{e}^{-1-4x}) \\  & =4({x}^{3}+{e}^{-1-4x}).\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a General Exponential Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={4}^{u},\,u=2x-{x}^{3}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}={4}^{u}\ln(4),\,\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=2-3{x}^{2}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}\cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} \\ & ={4}^{u}\ln(4)\cdot (2-3{x}^{2}) \\ & =(2-3{x}^{2})\cdot {4}^{u}\ln(4) \\ & =(2-3{x}^{2})\cdot {4}^{2x-{x}^{3}}\ln(4).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at $x=1$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\big|_{x=1} & =(2-3(1)^{2})\cdot {4}^{2(1)-(1)^{3}}\ln(4) \\ & =-1\cdot {4}^{1}\ln(4) \\ & =- 4 \ln{\left(4 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $x=1$ is $- 4 \ln{\left(4 \right)}.$

knowledge_point.title: Solving an Inhibited Decay Model

question.:question/problem:
A pork leg is taken out of the oven with a temperature of ${149}^{∘}C,$ and placed in a room that maintains a temperature of ${20}^{∘}C$, and its temperature begins to decrease. After $4$ minutes, the  temperature of the pork leg is ${132}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the pork leg to have a temperature of ${101}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature reading $T(t)$ of the pork leg decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the pork leg was transferred into the ${20}^{∘}C$ room.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={20}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-20).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-20} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-20} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-20| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-20>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-20 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-20 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-20 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =20+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the pork leg was ${149}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=149,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}149 & =20+K{e}^{0} \\ 149 & =20+K \\ K & =129\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=20+129{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $4$ minutes, the temperature of the pork leg is ${132}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(4)=132,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}132 & =20+129{e}^{-4k} \\ 112 & =129{e}^{-4k} \\ \frac{112}{129} & ={e}^{-4k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{112}{129}\right) & =-4k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{112}{129}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the pork leg has a temperature of ${101}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =101 \\ 20+129{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =101 \\ 129{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =81 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{27}{43} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{27}{43}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{27}{43}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the pork leg will have a temperature of ${101}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{27}{43}\right)}{-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{112}{129}\right)}≈13\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

knowledge_point.title: Separating the Variables in a Differential Equation

question.:question/problem:
Separate the variables in the following differential equation: 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x-3y}
$$

Work on an open domain where all displayed expressions are defined and the dependent-variable factor is nonzero. Choose an equivalent equation in the form $A(y)\, \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=B(x)$, with a multiplier depending only on $y$ and a right-hand side depending only on $x$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Expose the independent-variable and dependent-variable factors:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x-3y}={e}^{x}\cdot \frac{1}{{e}^{3y}}.
$$

Multiply both sides by the reciprocal of the dependent-variable factor. On the stated domain, this gives

$$
{e}^{3y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}.
$$

The derivative multiplier depends only on $y$ and the right-hand side only on $x$.

knowledge_point.title: Determining the Equation of a Wide Ellipse

question.:question/problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/edb-math/repairs/2026-10-27-topic-audit-2/published-probe/17592186087839/cd68f3e72f8d152bfe1c9ba160ae1d1dbd4e7bb93a26219e3fea36355f850f83.png)

What is the equation of the ellipse given above?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the horizontal radius has length $a=\frac{11}{2}$ and the vertical radius has length $b=2.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{5.5}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{\left(\frac{11}{2}\right)}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{\left(\frac{{11}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}\right)}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{\left(\frac{121}{4}\right)}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{4{x}^{2}}{121}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
